theory.intro: Spinning a region between a curve and the $y$-axis about the $y$-axis makes each slice a disc of radius $|x|$. So the rule is rearranged to give $x^{2}$ in terms of $y$, and the limits are $y$ values: $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$.
facts: The radius of each disc is $|x|$, so the integrand is $x^{2}$ written in terms of $y$.
Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject before integrating.
The limits are $y$ values, and using the $x$ values from the question instead is the most common error.
A limit given as an $x$ value is converted to a $y$ value by substituting it into the rule.
Volume is measured in cubic units, written $\text{units}^{3}$.
steps: Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$.
Identify the limits as the $y$ values $c$ and $d$.

workedExamples.solution_text:
At the $y$-axis, $x=0$, so $y=5$. Between $y=2$ and $y=5$, the radius is $|x|=5-y$.
$\begin{align*}x^{2}&=(5-y)^{2}\\V&=\pi\int_{2}^{5}(5-y)^{2}\,dy\\&=\pi\left[-\frac{(5-y)^{3}}{3}\right]_{2}^{5}\\&=\pi\left(0-(-9)\right)\\&=9\pi\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

At $x=3$, $y=3^{2}-3=6$, so the limits are $y=-3$ and $y=6$.
$\begin{align*}x^{2}&=y+3\\V&=\pi\int_{-3}^{6}(y+3)\,dy\\&=\pi\left[\frac{y^{2}}{2}+3y\right]_{-3}^{6}\\&=\pi\left(36-\left(-\frac{9}{2}\right)\right)\\&=\frac{81\pi}{2}\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

Write the squared radius in terms of $y$.
$\begin{align*}x&=y^{1/3}\\x^{2}&=y^{2/3}\\V&=\pi\int_{0}^{27}y^{2/3}\,dy\\&=\pi\left[\frac{3}{5}y^{5/3}\right]_{0}^{27}\\&=\frac{3\pi}{5}(243)\\&=\frac{729\pi}{5}\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

Rearrange for $x$, then square and expand before integrating.
$\begin{align*}y^{2}&=x-2\\x&=y^{2}+2\\x^{2}&=y^{4}+4y^{2}+4\\V&=\pi\int_{0}^{1}\left(y^{4}+4y^{2}+4\right)\,dy\\&=\pi\left[\frac{y^{5}}{5}+\frac{4y^{3}}{3}+4y\right]_{0}^{1}\\&=\pi\left(\frac{1}{5}+\frac{4}{3}+4\right)\\&=\frac{83\pi}{15}\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

Use the inverse relationship between logarithms and exponentials.
$\begin{align*}x&=e^{y}\\x^{2}&=e^{2y}\\V&=\pi\int_{0}^{2}e^{2y}\,dy\\&=\pi\left[\frac{e^{2y}}{2}\right]_{0}^{2}\\&=\frac{\pi}{2}\left(e^{4}-1\right)\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

At the $y$-axis, $y(y-4)=0$, giving $y=0$ and $y=4$. Between these limits, $x\leq0$, so the radius is $|x|=y(4-y)$.
$\begin{align*}x^{2}&=y^{2}(4-y)^{2}\\&=y^{4}-8y^{3}+16y^{2}\\V&=\pi\int_{0}^{4}\left(y^{4}-8y^{3}+16y^{2}\right)\,dy\\&=\pi\left[\frac{y^{5}}{5}-2y^{4}+\frac{16y^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{4}\\&=\pi\left(\frac{1024}{5}-512+\frac{1024}{3}\right)\\&=\frac{512\pi}{15}\ \text{units}^{3}\end{align*}$

foundation.solution_text:
1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y=2x$
$x=\dfrac{y}{2}$
$x^{2}=\dfrac{y^{2}}{4}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{4}\dfrac{y^{2}}{4}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{3}}{12}\right]_{0}^{4}$
$= \dfrac{16\pi}{3}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x^{2}=y$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{9}y\,dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{0}^{9}$
$= \dfrac{81\pi}{2}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=y^{\frac{1}{3}}$
$x^{2}=y^{\frac{2}{3}}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{8}y^{\frac{2}{3}}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{3}{5}y^{\frac{5}{3}}\right]_{0}^{8}$
$= \dfrac{3\pi}{5}\times 32$
$= \dfrac{96\pi}{5}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=y-1$
$x^{2}=(y-1)^{2}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{1}^{3}(y-1)^{2}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{(y-1)^{3}}{3}\right]_{1}^{3}$
$= \pi\left(\dfrac{8}{3}-0\right)$
$= \dfrac{8\pi}{3}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y=4-x^{2}$
$x^{2}=4-y$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{1}^{4}(4-y)dy$
$= \pi\left[4y-\dfrac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{4}$
$= \pi\left(8-\dfrac{7}{2}\right)$
$= \dfrac{9\pi}{2}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=y^{2}$
$x^{2}=y^{4}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{2}y^{4}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{5}}{5}\right]_{0}^{2}$
$= \dfrac{32\pi}{5}\ \text{units}^{3}$

development.solution_text:
1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=\dfrac{y-1}{2}$
$x^{2}=\dfrac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{1}^{7}\dfrac{(y-1)^{2}}{4}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{(y-1)^{3}}{12}\right]_{1}^{7}$
$= \pi\left(\dfrac{216}{12}-0\right)$
$= 18\pi\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=e^{y}$
$x^{2}=e^{2y}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{1}e^{2y}dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{e^{2y}}{2}\right]_{0}^{1}$
$= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\left(e^{2}-1\right)\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y=\dfrac{1}{x^{2}}$
$x^{2}=\dfrac{1}{y}$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{1}^{4}\dfrac{1}{y}dy$
$= \pi\left[\ln y\right]_{1}^{4}$
$= \pi\ln 4$
$= 2\pi\ln 2\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x^{2}=y$
2. **Identify the limits as the $y$ values $c$ and $d$**
The points $(1,1)$ and $(2,4)$ give $y=1$ and $y=4$.
3. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{1}^{4}y\,dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{2}}{2}\right]_{1}^{4}$
$= \pi\left(8-\dfrac{1}{2}\right)$
$= \dfrac{15\pi}{2}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=\dfrac{8-y}{2}$
$x^{2}=\dfrac{(8-y)^{2}}{4}$
2. **Identify the limits as the $y$ values $c$ and $d$**
The $x$-axis gives $y=0$ and the $y$-intercept gives $y=8$.
3. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{8}\dfrac{(8-y)^{2}}{4}dy$
$= \pi\left[-\dfrac{(8-y)^{3}}{12}\right]_{0}^{8}$
$= \pi\left(0+\dfrac{512}{12}\right)$
$= \dfrac{128\pi}{3}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y=x^{2}-2$
$x^{2}=y+2$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{-2}^{2}(y+2)dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{2}}{2}+2y\right]_{-2}^{2}$
$= \pi\left(6-(-2)\right)$
$= 8\pi\ \text{units}^{3}$

mastery.solution_text:
1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y=\dfrac{x^{2}}{4}$
$x^{2}=4y$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{4}4y\,dy$
$= \pi\left[2y^{2}\right]_{0}^{4}$
$= 32\pi\ \text{cm}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$x=y(y-2)$
$x^{2}=y^{2}(y-2)^{2}=y^{4}-4y^{3}+4y^{2}$
2. **Identify the limits as the $y$ values $c$ and $d$**
At the $y$-axis, $y(y-2)=0$, so $y=0$ or $y=2$.
For $0\leq y\leq2$, $x\leq0$, so the radius is $|x|=y(2-y)$.
3. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{2}\left(y^{4}-4y^{3}+4y^{2}\right)dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{5}}{5}-y^{4}+\dfrac{4y^{3}}{3}\right]_{0}^{2}$
$= \pi\left(\dfrac{32}{5}-16+\dfrac{32}{3}\right)$
$= \dfrac{16\pi}{15}\ \text{units}^{3}$

1. **Rearrange the rule to make $x^{2}$ the subject in terms of $y$**
$y^{2}=x-1$
$x=y^{2}+1$
$x^{2}=y^{4}+2y^{2}+1$
2. **Evaluate $V=\pi\int_{c}^{d}x^{2}\,dy$**
$V=\pi\int_{0}^{2}\left(y^{4}+2y^{2}+1\right)dy$
$= \pi\left[\dfrac{y^{5}}{5}+\dfrac{2y^{3}}{3}+y\right]_{0}^{2}$
$= \pi\left(\dfrac{32}{5}+\dfrac{16}{3}+2\right)$
$= \dfrac{206\pi}{15}\ \text{units}^{3}$
